text: We think about this a lot, honestly — Ellie and I go back and forth on strategy most weeks. Our whole approach is built around agencies feeling like the software understands their world, not some generic scheduling tool bolted on. Winning for us looks like being the obvious choice for a coordinator who's sick of spending her day on a rota. We talk about capabilities a lot too — support, compliance, the model work Dan's been doing. It's less a fixed plan than something we keep revisiting as customers tell us what actually matters to them.

I'm honestly not sure which option this is pointing at — that structuring work happens with Ellie and Priya, and I only see it once it's turned into something for me to build. So I can't say what conditions they've set for it to work; I've not been in those sessions and nobody's written the assumptions down anywhere I've seen. If you asked me about the engineering side of a decision I'd have an answer, but the framing itself isn't something I've had reason to look into yet.

The way this usually breaks for us is onboarding backing up and support drowning. If we take on agencies faster without anyone owning that handoff, tickets pile up and the compliance checks are the first thing that slips because they're already the flakiest part. It's not one clean disaster, it's just everything getting slower until an agency notices and gets annoyed. Dan flagged something similar back in the spring when we added two agencies in the same month and support couldn't keep up. That's probably the shape it takes again, just bigger.

Honestly I have opinions but not much evidence here. I know the incumbents exist and agencies complain about them, but we've never done a proper comparison — nobody's gone through and mapped what CareLineLive or a plain spreadsheet setup actually fails at against what our customers tell us afterwards. It's tangled up with why people leave a system too, which we haven't tracked properly either. Until someone follows a coordinator through a whole rota cycle on their old tool, I'm working off things people have said to me in passing rather than anything I'd stand behind.

Why - because coordinators were losing most of a day each week just building the rota, that's the number we always quote, though I think it was Dan who first timed it precisely. Who - the coordinator herself, not the registered manager, she's the one under the Friday deadline. How - by cutting that day down to something closer to an hour, though the exact figure moves around depending who you ask and which agency. What - the rota tool and the compliance check underneath it, that's really the two things we sell as one.

It's the thing that keeps agencies up at night, honestly — rotas and compliance both. Coordinators feel it, owners feel it when CQC comes round, carers feel it if a shift's wrong. Marek was talking about this back in the spring, how much anxiety just sits around the paperwork side even when nothing's actually gone wrong yet. Nobody solving it means the whole sector keeps running on people's goodwill and long evenings, which isn't sustainable for a coordinator doing it manually forever. It's a real drag on the industry, not just an inconvenience.

That's really more Ellie's territory than mine — product sits with her. But if I think about the compliance checking piece, since that's half of what I do, I'd say yes, there's probably two or three ways in: we could keep pushing the automated flagging we've built, or we could go simpler and just tighten the checklist templates coordinators use by hand. Ellie and Priya were going back and forth on this in a call a few weeks back, I want to say March, and I don't remember which way it landed. So take my read with a pinch of salt.

I don't have a clean answer to that one, actually — we don't run this consistently across every request that comes in. Sometimes I push on why, sometimes I just take the ask at face value and hand it to Dan or Ellie to weigh up. There's no process behind it yet, it's more instinct depending how the call's going. I'd need to actually track which requests got that follow-up and which didn't before I could tell you whether it changes what we end up building.

That's really Ellie's map more than mine, but the way she's put it to us, the whole thing rests on coordinators trusting the model's rota suggestions enough to actually use them instead of just rebuilding by hand. Riskiest bit, she reckons, is whether it holds up against a busy coordinator on a bad day — four of eleven have turned it on so far, and none of us have properly compared its picks against what a good coordinator would build. I think that's the one that could unravel the whole pitch.

When compliance checking goes wrong we usually just work through it as it comes up, checking the training records against what the agency's got on file. It's usually me or Dan who ends up looking at it, and sometimes Ellie if there's a product angle to it. There isn't really one particular file or thread we go back to for this, it depends on the agency and what's missing that week. We generally just sort it as it comes rather than write it up afterwards, so there's nothing tidy I could point you to.

I don't have a single day I can point to, and I've stopped trying to force one — the real shift for us was gradual, stitched together from separate conversations, and I never went back to timestamp which one actually flipped it. It's tangled up with Priya's calls, Marek's support tickets, things Dan noticed in usage logs — nobody's pulled that timeline into one place, so the honest answer is I can't isolate the moment, only that by a certain point we all agreed something had changed.

All four show up, but push is the one I hear loudest on calls — it's the coordinator losing most of a day to the rota, every time. Pull is easy, that's our pitch: cut that day down. Anxiety's real too, mostly about handing over three years of training records for an inspection, that's what stalls a signature. Habit is CareLineLive, or just paper if they're smaller. There was a call — February, I think — where a prospect said almost exactly that to me, though I'd have to check who it was before naming her.

I can't answer that properly because we've never run the two-sided version of this question on anyone — we ask "what do you like" and "what's missing," but not "how would you feel if this went away," which is a different thing entirely. It's been on my list since roughly the autumn and kept losing to actual bugs. Until I put both halves of that question to a handful of agencies directly, I'd just be inventing their reaction from what I already believe, which isn't the same as knowing it.

That one sits outside my patch—I'm mostly onboarding and compliance checks once an agency's already signed up. Ellie spent some time last spring looking at why the market hadn't moved before us, but I wasn't part of those conversations. What I notice from the coordinator side is people are relieved to have something that isn't a spreadsheet anymore, but the actual reason it took this long isn't something I've got a handle on. Priya would give you a proper answer on this one, not me.

I don't have an actual answer to that, in the sense of something we've put on paper. We talk in commercial terms — what agencies ask for, what they complain about — not in this language, and none of us has properly laid the four capabilities out against each other and argued where each sits from novel through to commodity. Dan's raised doing something like that a couple of times and it's kept sliding off the list because nothing was on fire. So what I've got is a lived sense of it from calls, not a map I could show you or defend under questioning.

I haven't really worked out where that lands, to be honest — it's not something I've mapped for our own team, and I don't think anyone has written down whose resistance it actually is versus who's just busy. It'd probably need someone going through the sales notes and the support tickets side by side to see where the same objection keeps recurring, and nobody has made that comparison yet as far as I know.

That's really Priya and Ellie's call, not something I've been part of shaping. What I notice from onboarding is that every agency we bring on has basically the same compliance headaches — training records, DBS checks, the same panic before an inspection. That repetition feels like it means something, like there's a proper niche there rather than us just picking up whoever answers the phone. Whether it's big enough on paper, or what comes after it, isn't something anyone's walked me through. I just see the pattern from the inside, agency after agency, and it looks consistent to me.

I don't have a clean name for who's annoyed by this — we don't systematically track why a prospect walks, so what I've got is impressions from calls, not a list. I know API integrations with clinical record systems come up and we say no, and I know that costs us something. Whether that's three deals a year or fifteen, I've never gone back through the notes to count. It's also something Ellie and I keep half-arguing about — whether to make the no explicit as policy or keep deciding it call by call. Neither of us has actually written it down yet.

What it earns us is trust inside a network that's basically closed to outsiders — home-care owners talk to each other, at regional CQC forums, in WhatsApp groups I'm not even in. Four of our eleven customers came through somebody else's recommendation, not a cold call, and that's not something you can buy with ad spend against CareLineLive. I think it's four, maybe five — I'd need to look at the sign-up notes properly. But that word-of-mouth credibility in a small, suspicious market is the real thing we're building, not just the software.

This one's not a quick fix, I reckon — it's the compliance checking again. We've patched it three separate times without ever touching how training records actually get stored, so at some point patching stops being honest. I'd call it a full cycle, maybe six weeks if Dan scopes it tight, though he'd probably push back on that number. There was an export that broke for two agencies right before an inspection back in the autumn — that's roughly when I stopped believing another patch would hold.

I don't know the answer to this one properly. I've never looked at how the suggestion feature actually threads through the system — I see it from the support queue end, after something's already gone wrong for an agency, not from the architecture side. Dan and Ellie built it and would know where it sits and what it touches. Nobody's walked me through the interactions, so I'd just be inventing a path if I tried to describe it, and I'd rather say that than make something up that sounds tidy.

Whenever we build something new, the real risk is always on the customer side — will they trust it, will they actually use it day to day. That's been true with the model behind rota suggestions too. Marek picked up a bit of feedback on it back in February, mostly agencies asking how it decides what it decides. I think as long as we're upfront about how it works and don't oversell it, most of that risk settles itself. It's more about managing expectations in the sales conversation than a technical thing we need to lock down in advance.

Ellie runs that conversation, not me — I just hear the outcome. This cycle it was: no bespoke integrations for a single agency, and nobody touches the core compliance logic while the model's still being tested on those four accounts. I think she also ruled out anything that pulls Marek off onboarding, since that's already stretched thin. She pinned it in our shared doc sometime in the last month or so, though I couldn't give you the exact date.

Whether there's an actual rule for this, I'm honestly unsure — I think it's still something Ellie and Dan go back and forth on rather than a decision that's been made. From where I sit, compliance fixes just get folded into whatever's shipping because customers are already on the phone about it, so the fixed window rarely survives contact with support. It's not written down anywhere I've seen, and it isn't mine to settle — I'd need to ask one of them rather than guess at it.

We do the exercise more as a habit than a finished thing — writing the release forces us to say what we're actually building for, rather than just shipping features. Marek and I tried it back in October for the compliance side, and it was useful, but it changed so much afterwards that I wouldn't call it a fixed document anymore. Mostly what it says shifts depending on which problem we're most anxious about that quarter — right now it'd lean towards the audit trail work, but ask me again after another inspection comes through and it'll probably read differently.

I don't have a real answer to most of this beyond the buying part, and even there I've never broken it out properly — conversion by call type, whether it's the compliance pitch or the price that lands. Usability, feasibility, whether it works across the business — those live with Dan, Ellie and Marek, and we haven't sat together and gone through Cagan's four risks as a set for Ashvale specifically. It's not that nobody cares, it's that we've been reacting deal to deal rather than stepping back to ask it properly. I'd need to pull the last few losses together to even start.

The honest candidate is coordinator hours on the rota — that's what agencies measure themselves against, and it's the number Priya leads with on every call. But we've never actually tested whether that's what they'd pay more for, because pricing sits flat at £340 regardless of size. My real guess, and it is a guess, is it's somewhere between rota time and audit readiness — a few agencies have told Priya they'd pay more if compliance checks tightened up. So I couldn't point to one clean metric; it's more like two candidates we've never separated properly.

That's really Priya's territory, she's the one on the sales calls. But from what I've picked up, we're flat at £340 a month across the board, no per-feature pricing — so willingness to pay by feature isn't something we've split out. I think she asked one of the bigger agencies about paying more for the compliance module maybe two months back, but I'm fuzzy on exactly when. She'd give you a straighter answer than me.

I can't put a name to it yet, because we've never tested the four categories against our own numbers. We don't have willingness-to-pay data, we don't have a proper account of why the couple of customers who churned actually left, and nobody's compared our pricing or roadmap against Ramanujam's model directly. It might be a mix rather than one clean answer, which is exactly the kind of thing I'd need real research to untangle rather than a guess on a call. Until we've done win-loss interviews and looked hard at usage against price, I'm not going to pretend I know which one fits.

I genuinely can't speak to this properly—it's Priya's side of the business, and I don't think she's ever written it down deal by deal. I know the rough shape from conversations: coordinator hurts, owner or manager pays. But whether that split holds across all eleven agencies, or whether some of the smaller ones have one person doing both, nobody's tracked. It'd mean going back through her notes on every account, and as far as I know that hasn't happened yet.

Onboarding is where I spend most of my time, and it's mostly fine — agencies get through it without dragging on support too much these days. The thing that keeps coming back round is compliance checking breaking after go-live, which eats into whatever goodwill we built during onboarding. I think of that as the real drag on the relationship, more than anything to do with pricing or upgrades. Dan and Priya would have a clearer view on how that maps to retention numbers than I would — that side sits more with them than with me.

Margins are good, that's the general feeling around here — Dan went through the cost side back in September and came away pretty happy with where we sat. Whether it's high for the right reason is more a founders'-call conversation, because it touches pricing and how much support load we're quietly carrying. Since we don't tier the price, whatever sits underneath the number gets spread the same way across every agency regardless of size. I'd call it solid, but I'm saying that from the product side, not from having built the spreadsheet myself.

I don't have a clean answer to that. We've never sat back and asked which model tells the story best — we picked flat pricing early because it was simple to sell, and we've just kept talking about it differently as the product's changed, without treating that as a version we'd count. So I couldn't put a number on how many times it's shifted this year; nobody's kept a log of the pitch itself, only of the actual price, which hasn't moved. It's the kind of thing I'd only be able to answer honestly after going back through call notes.

We don't run a free tier — it's a thirty-day trial with full access, so honestly nobody's ever priced what a lapsed trial costs us. Roughly it's Marek's onboarding hours plus whatever support tickets come in before they buy or drop off. If pushed, I'd guess somewhere between £150 and £300 a trial, depending how much hand-holding they needed. Three or four have run the whole month and never converted, though I'm not fully sure that count's right — Marek would know better than me. We've never worked out a usage point where one tips into loss; we're not metered enough for that yet.

That's really Priya's process, not mine — I sit in support, so I'm reconstructing this from what I've overheard on her calls. The pricing sheet says £340 flat, no tiers, but there's a step where she'll shave a month off if someone's stalling on the contract, and that bit's nowhere in writing. I want to say that's happened four, maybe five times this year, but I'm going from memory of conversations in the kitchen, not a log anywhere. You'd get a much cleaner answer out of her than out of me.

Contractually it's always been the registered manager at the agency — CQC holds them accountable, not us, and every deal I close makes that plain. Where it gets less clean is the rota model: four agencies now have it switched on, and one manager rang me straight out asking who's liable if it suggests a carer whose DBS has lapsed. I told her the sign-off is still hers. But I think Ellie was meant to tighten that language in the terms a few months back, maybe around spring, and I honestly haven't checked whether it landed.

It's something Ellie and I talk through whenever a new agency asks about data security — they want reassurance nobody outside their organisation can see their carers' records, and we point to everything being tenant-scoped from day one. It's held up fine so far, nobody's raised a leak or a breach. Internally we've kept access pretty tight too, more out of habit than any written policy. Marek flagged something about admin access back in the spring, I think, but as far as I know it didn't go anywhere after that.

That's really more compliance territory than something HIPAA or financial-services rules touch for us — different jurisdiction, different pressure. What matters to our agencies is that the trail backs up whatever an inspector asks for, and we built it around that instinct rather than any fixed checklist. Ellie pushed for stricter logging back in February after a support ticket rattled her, and it's been tightening since. It's less about a retention number and more about nothing getting silently overwritten. Priya tends to field the reassurance conversation with customers directly, so I mostly hear about it secondhand from her.

It's on AWS, eu-west-1, so London region — that's where the database's lived since we built the thing. As for who's told the customer, I think it's baked into the contract terms Priya sends, and Marek usually walks through it in onboarding, though I'm not certain he says it every single time. There's a data processing addendum we drafted last year that spells it all out, but I doubt many of the eleven have actually sat and read it properly.

Honestly I haven't got a real picture of this. None of our eleven have been running us alongside an incumbent for anything like two years — our oldest customer is eleven months in, so the long tail of coexistence is still theoretical for us. Whether it gets messier around inspection time, with evidence split across two systems, or whether agencies just quietly stop bothering with the old one — nobody's tracking that yet because it hasn't happened long enough to watch. That's a question for whoever's still there in a year, not one I can answer from calls.

That line honestly isn't drawn yet. We've talked about it — training records versus DBS status versus something like a carer's health declaration — but we haven't agreed which ones we'd stand behind saying 'the system won't call this, only a person can' versus which we'll quietly add coverage for over time. Part of it is we're still learning which gaps actually get flagged in practice, since we've only got a handful of months of real usage across eleven agencies to look at. Until we've seen more inspections come through customers who use us, I don't think we can commit to a firm boundary.

Integration's not really something I deal with day to day, so I can only speak broadly. We take in whatever the agency already has — client and carer information — and we're careful around anything touching compliance records, because that's the part inspectors care about. Dan and Ellie had a long back-and-forth about this earlier in the year, I want to say around March, but I wasn't really part of those conversations. From onboarding's side, what matters most is getting data in cleanly at the start; what happens underneath that is above my pay grade.

We've never really untangled goal, signal and metric the way this question implies — on sales calls we jump straight to a number because that's what closes a deal in the moment. Working out what we're actually trying to achieve, versus what's just easy to count, hasn't happened; it needs time away from calls that I haven't carved out. Dan and Ellie have talked about wanting a proper framework for this on the product side, but from the commercial end it's still instinct and whatever renewal numbers we've got to hand.

The thing customers actually feel is compliance — whether we catch a missing training record before an inspector does. That's the bit they mention on calls, more than speed. Marek hears it most, since he's in the onboarding conversations, and he says it comes up almost every time. We haven't picked apart which single number represents that best, but it's clearly tied up with trust rather than just hours saved. Ellie's been circling around defining something more formal for a while, but nothing's landed yet.

I don't have a proper answer here — nobody's worked through what gaming the rota-time number would actually look like in practice, so there's no counter-metric attached to it. With only four agencies on the model so far, we haven't seen behaviour that looks like manipulation, but that's not the same as having checked. It's the kind of guardrail question we owe ourselves before this goes wider than eleven agencies. Until someone goes through the data asking what a coordinator could fake to hit a good time, I wouldn't want to name what the catch should be.

I don't have a fixed line for that, and I'm not sure I've let myself think about it properly. We're revenue-funded, no board pushing us toward a deadline, so there's never been a moment that forced the four of us to say it out loud. If the compliance side kept breaking the way it has, or the model never really proved itself, that might edge me there — but I couldn't put a date on either, because we haven't tracked either closely enough to know what changing would even look like.

If more than half the four agencies who've turned the model on switched it back off within a month, I'd call that a stop signal. I remember Dan mentioning a threshold too — two complaints before we freeze the rollout — but that number came from a conversation, not something we wrote down, so I might have it slightly wrong.

I don't have a real answer to that one yet, if I'm honest — it's not a question we've put to ourselves feature by feature. We argue about priorities constantly, but always forward-looking: what to build next, not whether something we already built earns its keep. There's no framework sitting behind our roadmap that would let me test each piece against "would we start this now." I'd need to go through the product line by line with Dan and Priya and score each part against what it costs us to maintain versus what it's winning us, and that exercise hasn't happened.

I don't know, and it's not something anyone's separated out on my end — nobody in support has gone back and checked whether this climbs because we improved something or just because more agencies signed on and more weeks went by. It's exactly the shape of thing that could go up on its own. Ellie's raised that worry about a couple of our other numbers before, so I wouldn't be surprised if this one's the same, but I've never sat with the actual data to test it myself.

Honestly, there isn't a proper eval yet, not one with a fixed set we run every time. What passes for one right now is Dan looking at a handful of rotas and judging whether the suggestion is close enough, and none of that's written down anywhere I could point to. We haven't agreed what a fair benchmark would even be — real coordinator-built rotas, or something we construct — so there's no pass rate I'd stand behind in a customer conversation. It's a gap I'd like sorted before we lean on it commercially.

Honestly that's more Marek and Priya's ground than mine — they're closest to what customers actually flag. My sense is the compliance side gets looked at pretty thoroughly, and model suggestions get a look before anything reaches a live rota. It's less a formal process, more the four of us keeping an eye on things as they surface. Marek was into some edge cases around February, but what came out of that sits with him, not me — I just build the thing, I'm not the one checking it against reality afterwards.

We do talk about this a fair bit—Ellie raised it in a product sync, back around when the model first went live, and the feeling was it needs to earn its place before we widen it further. What I mostly hear from agencies is whether the suggested rota felt right, not whether the compliance checks underneath were accurate. So my sense of it comes from support calls, not anything formal. Dan's closer to what's actually being measured on the technical side, so that's really his call to make.

The clearest failure we've seen is the model suggesting a carer whose DBS check had lapsed — that was back in, I think, October, and the coordinator caught it before publishing. Visibility depends entirely on someone checking every line against the compliance record, which right now means Marek or whoever's handling that agency's onboarding doing a spot-check. Who actually pays: financially it's the agency, in a CQC finding, not us — but reputationally it's ours, we'd lose the account. Only four agencies have it switched on, so the exposure's small, but it's not nothing, and I don't think we've been rigorous about testing it.

There isn't a straight answer I can give you on this yet. Whether the review coordinators do is a real check or just a rubber stamp because they're rushed — we've never tested it. Nobody's tracked how often a coordinator actually changes a suggested rota versus just clicking through, and until the model's used a lot more widely that data barely exists. It's come up in conversation more than once, usually when someone's uneasy about the model growing, but we haven't worked out what "real control" would even look like to measure against. So it's a fair question, and one I can't answer properly yet.

I don't have a proper answer to this. We know there's a coordinator between the model and anything a carer sees, but we've never mapped what happens if a bad suggestion slipped past that — whether it's contained to one carer's shift or cascades through a week's rota, and how you'd unwind it once it's live. There's no severity scale, no rollback process written down. It's sat on my list since we're about to open the feature to more agencies, but right now it's a gap because nobody's asked it of us yet, not because we've decided the answer.

I don't have a real answer here, and I'd be making it up if I gave you one. Cost per action isn't something I've ever been asked to track, and with only four agencies running the model, there isn't enough usage yet to say anything meaningful about scale. Dan would know the inference side, and even he'd need to weigh it against how often coordinators actually keep the suggestion versus override it, which nobody's measured either. It's genuinely not landed on anyone's desk as a question to answer yet, mine included.

For the rota suggestion feature it's meant to be a couple of seconds, tops — Dan set that as the target when he first wired the model in. When it's slower, what I hear from calls is a coordinator just clicks away and does the shift manually, so we lose the moment. I had one prospect in March who timed it against her own gut feel and we lost that round on speed, not accuracy. I'd want Dan's actual number rather than my memory of it, but that's roughly where we sit.

That's Ellie's argument more than mine — she reckons the model bit is maybe a tenth of what we actually sell, the rest being the CQC-facing compliance records and the carer history we hold for eleven agencies. So if a big provider shipped a decent scheduler next release, we'd still have that trail sitting underneath it. I think that's roughly right, though I've never seen her set it out properly, and Priya's the one actually testing it against CareLineLive in real calls. Somewhere between a genuine moat and a story we tell ourselves — I lean toward the former, but I wouldn't bet the company on my own read of it.

The pitch is simple: agencies run rotas through us, that usage feeds the model, the model gets sharper, more agencies want it on — a flywheel. Four of our eleven have switched it on so far. Dan mentioned the retrain cycle runs something like every six weeks, though that's from memory and worth confirming with him directly. Honestly, at four customers it's more a hope than a proven loop — I say it in sales calls because it's the right shape of story, but we haven't got the volume yet to call it real. It's asserted, dressed as inevitable.

Two, maybe three wrong ones in a row, is my instinct — after that a coordinator just quietly stops opening the suggestion panel and goes back to doing it herself. One agency, I think it was Meadowfield, switched it off after a single bad shift clash, though Marek would know that story better than me. We haven't actually measured any of this, so treat it as a guess rather than something I'd want in a report with my name on it.

That's really an instrumentation question more than a sales one, but from where I sit, coordinators do say having the reasoning there makes the suggestion feel less like a black box — it comes up a lot in renewal calls. Ellie built the explanation panel with exactly that visibility in mind when the toggle shipped. Whether we're capturing the click before acceptance as its own event is more Dan's territory than mine. What I can tell you is trust in the feature has clearly gone up since we added the panel, and honestly that matters more to me than the mechanics of measuring the sequence.

Honestly, most of our ideas start the same way — someone's frustrated with a coordinator, we go and sit with an agency, and it comes out of that conversation rather than us dreaming it up in a room. Marek's usually the first to hear it, because he's in onboarding calls constantly, and he'll mention something back to the rest of us. Then Priya tells us whether anyone would actually pay for it. It's less a process than a habit we've built up since the early days, and it works well enough that we haven't tried to formalise it.

Nobody's actually framed it this way for us, as far as I know. We've spent most of our energy just getting compliance checking to stop breaking, so the question of what a brilliant experience looks like beyond 'reliable' hasn't had anyone's attention. There's no document, no whiteboard version I've seen, nothing. It would take Ellie or Priya sitting with a handful of agencies and asking them directly what would delight them, and that conversation hasn't happened yet. So I don't have a real answer for you there.

I don't have a good answer for this one, if I'm honest. The place it matters most right now is the model behind rota suggestions - four agencies have switched it on, and if it gets a shift wrong that's someone not turning up at a person's house. We haven't run anything that tells us how it compares to a coordinator doing it by hand, so I can't say the evidence matches the stakes. It's been raised in a couple of internal chats but nobody's built a way to actually measure it yet.

Honestly, I don't think we've asked it properly — the actual Sean Ellis scoring, everyone answered the same way and tallied up. Priya's had bits of that conversation on renewal calls, but nobody's put it into one sheet with a number on it. I build the thing rather than talk to customers about losing it, so it wouldn't be my job to know anyway. To answer it properly we'd need to run it as one survey across all eleven, and as far as I know that hasn't happened.
